flashcards.q: What are agents genuinely good at in architecture review?
flashcards.a: Consistency checks against a stated invariant across a large codebase, missing-case enumeration against a contract, first-draft ADR/design docs from noisy source material, and drift detection between docs and code -- all exhaustive search, not judgment.

flashcards.q: What are agents NOT good at in architecture review, and why?
flashcards.a: Judging whether a tradeoff is right for a specific org. That judgment depends on institutional memory (past outages, political compromises, customer contracts) that was never written down anywhere the agent could be shown, so no amount of better prompting fixes it.

flashcards.q: What is the one ADR field that must always be human-filled, and how do you enforce that?
flashcards.a: The 'Decision' field, requiring a named person, not agent-generated prose. Enforce with a CI check that fails a merge referencing an ADR whose Decision field is empty or unattributed.

flashcards.q: Name the failure mode when an agent generates a design doc from an existing codebase.
flashcards.a: Confident-description drift: the doc describes what the code LOOKS LIKE it does (based on names/comments/pattern) rather than what it actually does, fluently and with the same confidence whether right or wrong -- wrong exactly where the code is subtle, buggy, or stale.

flashcards.q: Why is same-model self-review of a design a weak strategy?
flashcards.a: A model reviewing its own output checks whether the design looks like the kind of thing generated correctly, not whether it matches reality -- the same weights rationalize the same shortcut twice.

flashcards.q: What mitigations define an effective adversarial design review?
flashcards.a: A different model family (not the same model twice), read-only access with no shared reasoning context, and an 'enumerate every failure mode' framing instead of 'is this good' (which invites agreement). The human still owns the final decision.

flashcards.q: How do you mechanically detect drift between a doc and its implementation?
flashcards.a: Extract every checkable factual claim from the doc, locate the actual implementing code for each, and report match/mismatch with file+line evidence. Track claims that could NOT be verified as a separate category from confirmed matches.

flashcards.q: Why must 'could not verify' never be collapsed into 'matches' in a drift-detection tool?
flashcards.a: Doing so reintroduces the exact confident-description failure the tool exists to catch, just moved one layer up -- a false 'confirmed' is worse than an honest 'unverified'.

flashcards.q: What is the estimated annual cost of documentation drift for a 50-person engineering team?
flashcards.a: Upward of $200K a year in wasted clarification time and decisions made against stale information -- a cost that compounds under agent-assisted development because commit velocity is higher.

flashcards.q: How much faster is agent-assisted ADR first-draft authoring versus manual writing?
flashcards.a: Roughly minutes versus the traditional 30-40 minutes of manual writing -- a real gain in authoring speed that says nothing about the quality of the underlying judgment.

flashcards.q: What is 'the accountability line' in AI-assisted architecture review?
flashcards.a: The agent does not own the decision, at any point, regardless of draft quality. This isn't a capability gap that improves with better models -- it's a governance requirement: a wrong architectural bet has consequences that must land on a named accountable person.

flashcards.q: Is PR-conformance-to-ADR automation ('does this PR obey accepted decisions') a solved problem?
flashcards.a: It's reliable for mechanical conformance (does this PR touch a frozen module) but not for judging whether the ADR itself still holds -- that's the same tradeoff-judgment problem moved one level up, and still needs a human periodic review.

flashcards.q: What's the standard for deciding an agent-generated design doc is trustworthy enough to build against?
flashcards.a: Line-by-line verification of every checkable claim against real code or a test, treated like an intern's first-week writeup of a system they didn't build: useful as structure, worthless as ground truth until confirmed.

flashcards.q: What is the Level 1/2/3 control distinction applied to an ADR's Decision field?
flashcards.a: Level 1 (a norm saying 'a human should decide') is an instruction that gets skipped under deadline pressure. Level 3 (a CI check that fails an empty/unattributed Decision field) is enforcement -- only Level 3 actually constrains behavior.

flashcards.q: If both models in an adversarial review agree a design is fine, is that strong evidence?
flashcards.a: Weaker than it sounds -- both models may share the same systematic blind spot in how they reason about a given problem class. Institutional memory about similar past efforts is still a check neither model result substitutes for.
